summary: Lays out a framework for PSAMP, a protocol for picking out some packets from a stream, forming reports about them, and exporting those reports to a collector. It describes the components involved, such as the selection steps, and how they fit together.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of writing down every car on a highway, you pick a few and record details about those. This note describes the parts of a system that chooses some network packets and reports on them.

questions: how does packet sampling and reporting work
subtitle: The building blocks for picking a few packets out of a stream, describing them, and shipping the reports to a collector.

tldr.problem: Operators need measurements of traffic across networks built from many vendors' equipment, but looking at every packet is too costly, and each vendor's way of choosing and reporting packets would differ.
tldr.mechanism: The PSAMP framework defines a Selection Process that picks packets, a Metering Process that builds reports on them, and an Exporting Process that sends the reports to a Collector, together with generic requirements for each step.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational framework that sets the vocabulary and requirements; the detailed selection techniques, export protocol and information model are in companion documents (RFC 5475, RFC 5476 and RFC 5477).

facts.label: Required export transport
facts.value: SCTP with Partial Reliability (UDP only within operator domains)

today: RFC 5474 is an Informational RFC from March 2009 and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The detailed techniques, protocol and information model are in RFC 5475, RFC 5476 and RFC 5477.

sections.title: Why a Packet Sampling Framework
sections.content:
RFC 5474 describes the PSAMP (Packet SAMPling) framework: how network elements select subsets of packets by statistical and other methods, and export a stream of reports on the selected packets to a Collector.

The motivation is measurement-based support for network management and control across multivendor domains. That calls for domain-wide consistency in the selection schemes on offer and in how the resulting measurements are presented and interpreted.

Despite the name, PSAMP selection is broader than sampling. It includes random selection, deterministic selection (filtering), and deterministic approximations to random selection (hash-based selection). The framework is one of a series: RFC 5475 covers the selection techniques, RFC 5476 the export protocol, and RFC 5477 the information model. In this document the words must, should and may are informational only.
sections.plainLanguage: If you want to know what kinds of cars use a road, you do not need to write down every car. This document says how to choose some packets fairly and report on them in a way every maker's equipment understands.

sections.title: The Three Processes and Their Terms
sections.content:
A stream of packets is watched at an Observation Point, such as a router port or a line to which a probe is attached. A Selection Process inspects each packet and decides whether to select it. The Selection Process is part of the Metering Process, which builds a report on each selected packet from its Packet Content and possibly other information, such as how the packet was treated or when it arrived. An Exporting Process then sends the reports to a Collector.

A Selector defines what the Selection Process does to one packet. A Composite Selector chains Selectors so that the output of one feeds the next; a Selector that is not composite is primitive. The Selection Process may keep Selection State, for example input sequence numbers, timestamps, pseudorandom number generator iterators, hash values and indicators of whether a Selector chose the packet.

The report output, the Report Stream, has two kinds of content: Packet Reports and Report Interpretation, the subsidiary information needed to read them. A PSAMP Device hosts at least an Observation Point, a Metering Process and an Exporting Process. The RFC prefers the word "stream" to "flow" because selected packets do not necessarily have a property that sets them apart from unselected ones. The PSAMP Metering Process is compared to the IPFIX Metering Process, with the difference that PSAMP always includes a Selection Process.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a factory line: a worker picks some items off the belt, another writes a note on each, and a third mails the notes to an office. Those are the selector, the meter and the exporter.

sections.title: Generic Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC lists lettered requirements. For selection: Selectors must be simple enough to run ubiquitously at maximal line rate, rich enough for a range of applications, extensible, able to handle IPv4, IPv6 and MPLS, and robust against packet streams crafted to evade selection or overload measurement systems. The protocol must support several independent Metering Processes at one host. Selectors that interpret packet fields must be configurable to ignore encrypted packets.

For reporting: the Report Stream must be self-defining, so no extra information has to be fetched from the Observation Point. It must allow loss to be detected, for example with sequence numbers, and must let accuracy be determined. Reported quantities must reflect the router state the packet met. Reports must conform with RFC 2804, so full packet capture of arbitrary streams is explicitly out of scope.

For exporting: buffering delays must be limitable, export across a network must be congestion avoiding, and secure export needs confidentiality, integrity and authenticity. Configuration must be easy and must be securable against unauthorized change and eavesdropping, because eavesdropping could help an attacker craft traffic that evades the measurement.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say the picking must be quick and fair, the notes must explain themselves, and the mail must not clog the roads or be read by strangers.

sections.title: Selection, Reporting and Export
sections.content:
PSAMP splits Selectors into two types. A filter selects deterministically from the packet content, its treatment, or the Selection State; examples are property match filtering and hash-based selection. Sampling is any Selector that is not a filter, either content-independent (systematic or uniform random) or content-dependent (for example, a probability that depends on port numbers). A PSAMP Selection Process must support at least one of: systematic count-based sampling, systematic time-based sampling, probabilistic n-out-of-N sampling, uniform probabilistic sampling, non-uniform probabilistic sampling, property match filtering, or hash-based selection. Useful composites are concatenated property match filters, filtering followed by sampling, and sampling followed by filtering.

Each primitive Selector must count packets presented at its input and include that count as a sequence number for selected packets. With sequence numbers s1 to sn on n received reports, the attained selection fraction is R = (n-1)/(sn-s1), and the bytes in the original stream are estimated as B/R, where B is the sum of the reported bytes. This works even when reports are lost.

Packet Reports must carry the input sequence numbers and the Metering Process identifier, and the Metering Process must support, as an option, a basic report of some contiguous bytes from the start of the packet. Extended reports may add protocol fields, interfaces, source and destination BGP AS, a timestamp (to microsecond resolution) and hash values. The Report Interpretation must give Selector configuration, report format and accuracy.

Export uses IPFIX. Export Packets must carry an Exporting Process identifier and a sequence number. Reliable export is not required; a congestion-aware unreliable transport may be used. IPFIX requires SCTP with the Partial Reliability Extension, and also allows UDP only within the operators' administrative domains. The Exporting Process must have a configurable export rate limit, must be able to close an Export Packet after one Packet Report to limit delay, and must have a configurable upper bound on delay before transmission, after which the Export Packet is dropped. Export Packets may be compressed if timeliness is kept.
sections.plainLanguage: You can pick every tenth car, or pick cars at random, or pick all red ones. Each pick is numbered so that, even if some notes get lost in the mail, you can still work out how many cars there really were.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
PSAMP shares IPFIX's export requirements and relies on IPFIX to meet them. A PSAMP Device may report some initial bytes of a packet, including part of the payload, which the RFC considers conformant with RFC 2804 because neither 1-in-1 sampling nor reporting a specific number of initial bytes is required. Packet Reports must be able to stay confidential in transit.

The main concern for hash-based selection is that related packets could be disproportionately selected, through unexpected hash behavior or deliberate crafting. Only cryptographic hash functions (for example, one based on MD5) with a private parameter are strong enough against all conceivable attacks, but they may be too costly at line rate, so PSAMP is not expected to standardize a cryptographic hash function at present. Since hash-based selection is deterministic, it is open to replay attacks, which changing parameters can mitigate. Hiding only the selected range is not enough: a private parameter must be used inside the hash function. Non-cryptographic functions such as CRC-32 can have their private parameter discovered from enough past selections.

Hash parameters must be kept private: not displayable in cleartext, not set remotely in cleartext over a channel that may be eavesdropped, and changed regularly. In a domain using trajectory sampling the changes must be synchronized. Default values should be initialized randomly.
sections.plainLanguage: If a cheater knows how you pick cars, they can sneak by unnoticed or flood your notebook. So the secret rule for picking has to stay secret and be changed often.

sections.title: Feasibility and Applications
sections.content:
The RFC argues PSAMP must be simple and cheap to implement, noting that sampling and filtering are already in available equipment. Filtering needs only a few mask, compare and range operations, counter-based sampling is a counter that is decremented and tested for zero, and a simple hash such as CRC maps well to hardware. A hash as complex as MD5 may be precluded at full line rate, though it can be feasible for a second hash computed only on selected packets.

Applications described include baseline measurement with drill down, where a new Metering Process is started on the same stream to filter an interesting subset; trajectory sampling, where all Observation Points use a common hash on path-invariant packet content so a packet is selected everywhere or nowhere; passive performance measurement, such as checking service level agreements; and troubleshooting, where packet reports can tell apart causes that aggregate link statistics cannot.
sections.plainLanguage: The picking tricks are simple enough for cheap equipment. Picking the same cars at every checkpoint lets you follow a car's whole trip and find where trouble starts.

viz.caption: SELECTORS A PSAMP SELECTION PROCESS CAN OFFER (AT LEAST ONE)

items.label: Systematic count-based sampling
items.desc: Selection is triggered periodically by packet count.

items.label: Systematic time-based sampling
items.desc: Selection is triggered at periodic instants separated by a spacing; packets within the interval length are selected.

items.label: Probabilistic n-out-of-N sampling
items.desc: From each count-based block of N packets, n are selected at random.

items.label: Uniform probabilistic sampling
items.desc: Packets are selected independently with fixed probability p.

items.label: Non-uniform probabilistic sampling
items.desc: Packets are selected independently with a probability p that depends on Packet Content.

items.label: Property match filtering
items.desc: A packet is selected if Field=Value.

items.label: Hash-based selection
items.desc: A hash of part of the Packet Content falls in a specified range.
